name: Japanese
region: Japan, plus large communities in Brazil, Hawaii and the US
about: Japanese mixes three scripts in one sentence: hiragana for grammar, katakana for foreign words, and kanji borrowed from Chinese. The verb always comes at the end, just like in Hindi, so sentence order will feel surprisingly familiar.
pronunciation: Japanese has only five vowels, a, i, u, e, o, said short and clean like in Hindi.
Long vowels, written with a line on top like ō, are held for twice as long and can change the meaning.
The r sound is a light tap between r and l, close to the soft Hindi sound in the middle of ladka.
Keep every syllable even and flat; Japanese uses pitch, not strong stress, so avoid punching one syllable.

lessons.intro: Konnichiwa! Today we start with the polite little words that open every door in Japan. Bow slightly as you say them, and you will already sound respectful.
lessons.tip: Japanese changes words by politeness level. With strangers, shopkeepers and elders, use the polite desu and masu endings. Bowing replaces handshakes, and a small nod of the head is perfectly fine for learners.

phrases.note: Konnichiwa is the standard hello for daytime. In the morning say ohayō gozaimasu, and in the evening say konbanwa.
O-genki desu ka means are you well. Japanese people use it when they have not seen someone for a while, not as an everyday greeting.
Genki desu means I am fine. To sound extra polite, add okagesama de at the start, which means thanks to you.

phrases.native: ありがとうございます。
phrases.note: Arigatō gozaimasu is the polite thank you. With close friends you can just say arigatō.
Sumimasen is the most useful word in Japan. It means excuse me, sorry, and even thank you for the trouble. For a real apology, say gomen nasai.
Sayōnara is a formal goodbye, often for longer partings. With friends say jā, mata ne, which means see you.

lessons.intro: Now let us introduce ourselves the Japanese way. Introductions here are short, polite and always end with a little bow.
lessons.tip: Japanese people usually drop watashi, meaning I, once it is clear who is speaking. Never add san after your own name; san is only for other people.

phrases.note: Watashi wa Puriya desu means I am Priya. In formal settings you can say Puriya to mōshimasu, which is more humble.
O-namae wa nan desu ka politely asks for someone's name. The o at the start makes the word name respectful.

phrases.native: どちらから来ましたか？
phrases.note: Dochira kara kimashita ka literally means which direction did you come from. Dochira is a polite way to say where.
Indo kara kimashita means I came from India. You can also say Indo-jin desu, which means I am Indian.

phrases.native: はじめまして。よろしくお願いします。
phrases.note: Hajimemashite means meeting you for the first time. Yoroshiku onegai shimasu adds please treat me kindly, and Japanese people almost always say both together.

phrases.native: 日本語が少し話せます。
phrases.note: Nihongo ga sukoshi hanasemasu means I can speak a little Japanese. Expect people to answer, jōzu desu ne, you are good at it!

lessons.intro: Time for numbers! Japanese counting is very regular, so once you learn one to ten, bigger numbers come easily.
lessons.tip: Four and seven each have two readings. Yon and nana are safer in daily life, because shi sounds like the word for death and is often avoided.

phrases.note: Ichi, ni, san, yon, go. Four is also read shi, but yon is the safer choice when counting.
Roku, nana, hachi, kyū, jū. Seven can also be shichi, and nine can be ku, especially when telling the time.
Ima nan-ji desu ka means what time is it now. Ji means o'clock, so three o'clock is san-ji.
Kyō means today. Keep the long o sound, because kyo with a short vowel sounds unclear.
Ashita means tomorrow. In formal speech you may also hear asu. Mata ashita means see you tomorrow.
Kinō means yesterday. Like today, it is used without any extra word for on.

lessons.intro: Let us go shopping and eat! Japanese food is wonderful, and a few polite phrases will make every meal and every shop easier.
lessons.tip: Bargaining is rare in Japan, and tipping is not expected; it can even confuse staff. Before eating say itadakimasu, and after the meal say gochisōsama deshita.

phrases.note: Kore wa ikura desu ka means how much is this. Point at the item as you say kore, which means this.
Chotto takasugimasu means it is a bit too expensive. Chotto softens the sentence, which Japanese people appreciate. Prices are usually fixed, so use it gently.
O-mizu o kudasai means water, please. In most restaurants cold water is free, so you can ask for it any time.

phrases.native: 私はベジタリアンです。
phrases.note: Watashi wa bejitarian desu means I am vegetarian. Many soups use fish stock called dashi, so also ask, dashi wa haitte imasu ka.
Totemo oishii desu means it is very delicious. Cooks love hearing it, and friends often just say oishii!

phrases.native: お会計をお願いします。
phrases.note: O-kaikei o onegai shimasu means the bill, please. In many restaurants you take the bill slip and pay at the counter near the door.

lessons.intro: Japan's trains are famous for being on time. Let us learn how to find the station and follow directions without getting lost.
lessons.tip: Kudasai after a verb turns it into a polite request, like please turn or please go. Big stations have many exits, so ask for the exit name too.

phrases.note: Eki wa doko desu ka means where is the station. Eki is the word for train station, and you will see it on signs everywhere.

phrases.native: 左に曲がってください。
phrases.note: Hidari ni magatte kudasai means please turn left. Hidari is left.

phrases.native: 右に曲がってください。
phrases.note: Migi ni magatte kudasai means please turn right. Migi is right.

phrases.native: まっすぐ行ってください。
phrases.note: Massugu itte kudasai means please go straight. Hold the double s and double t with a tiny pause.

phrases.native: ここからどのくらいですか？
phrases.roman: koko kara dono kurai desu ka?
phrases.note: Koko kara dono kurai desu ka means how far is it from here. People usually answer in minutes of walking rather than in kilometres.
Tasukete kudasai means please help me, and it is for real trouble. For small help, like asking the way, start with sumimasen instead.

lessons.intro: In our last lesson, we learn the phrases that keep a conversation going, even when you get a little lost. You have come so far!
lessons.tip: Japanese people often avoid a direct no. If you hear chotto, meaning a little, with a pause, it usually means no, politely.

phrases.note: Hai means yes, and iie means no. Hai also means I am listening, so it does not always mean agreement.
Wakarimasen means I don't understand. Say sumimasen first to sound softer.

phrases.native: ゆっくり話してください。
phrases.note: Yukkuri hanashite kudasai means please speak slowly. Yukkuri means slowly or relaxed.

phrases.native: これはどういう意味ですか？
phrases.roman: kore wa dō iu imi desu ka?
phrases.note: Kore wa dō iu imi desu ka means what does this mean. Imi is the word for meaning.
Suki desu means I like it. For something you just saw or tried, ki ni irimashita, meaning it has won me over, also sounds natural.
Oyasuminasai is good night, said before going to bed. With family and friends, just oyasumi is fine.
